title: Data centres in Ireland
voice: Every title, desc, comment or intro here is read by a player and is written as Envie speaking. See CLAUDE.md and _DESIGNS/envie-voice-and-text-rewrite-guide.md: plain short sentences, no em-dashes, European spelling, no emoji, facts and sources untouched. The optional 'envie' line on a slide is his own aside, one short sentence.

slides.text: Data centres in Ireland. Why is everyone talking about them?
Every time you stream a video, send an email or ask an AI a question, a server somewhere has to do the work. That server sits in a data centre.
slides.footer: It needs electricity to run, water to keep cool, materials to build. A lot of each. That's why it matters.

slides.caption: Around 4% of global greenhouse gas emissions already come from our digital lives, more than aviation. And it's growing fast as AI takes off, which means more data centres.
slides.envie: More than every plane in the sky. I didn't expect that.

slides.caption: Ireland has a lot of them. Around 25% of all European data centres are here. Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, they all built major operations in Ireland. Dublin has quietly become Europe's data capital.
slides.envie: One in four. On an island this size.

slides.caption: Powering those data centres took 22% of Ireland's entire electricity in 2025, up from almost nothing a decade ago.
slides.footer: For context, Ireland's entire peak national demand tops out at around 6,000 MW, and prospective new data centres are already requesting up to 5,800 MW.
slides.envie: That's a lot of electricity for storing photos.

slides.text: Is this a problem? The debate looks very different depending on where you are.
bullets: Iceland runs data centres on geothermal power. Not much concern there.
The UK has a more mixed grid and a different balance. There, the main worry right now is water.
slides.footer: Ireland's grid is still partly fossil-fuelled. Every new data centre competes for green energy that was meant to decarbonise homes and factories.

slides.text: Since 2015, nearly all growth in Ireland's electricity demand has come from data centres. The wind farms being built aren't replacing fossil fuels. They're just keeping up with new AI demand.
slides.footer: Between 2020 and 2023, only 16% of the extra data centre demand was matched by new renewable purchases. The rest came from the standard grid mix, gas and coal included.

slides.text: Ireland's grid is so strained that regulators have put a de facto stop on new connections in Dublin. New data centres must now build their own power generation or batteries before they can connect.
slides.footer: Because renewable energy comes and goes, many are turning to on-site gas turbines. Decarbonisation, meet the bypass.

slides.caption: New power demand for data centres isn't just an Irish problem. Globally it's projected to grow by 165% by 2030, with AI a big part of it.
slides.footer: But as AI gets more efficient, shouldn't demand fall?
slides.envie: So everyone's grid is asking the same question.

slides.text: When a technology gets more efficient, total consumption goes up, not down. It's called the Jevons Paradox.
slides.footer: Cheaper AI means more AI, everywhere. More efficient chips don't lower the electricity bill. They make it possible to build bigger systems that were too expensive to run before.
slides.envie: That one took me a minute.

slides.caption: But it's not all negative. Digital tools and AI could cut global greenhouse gas emissions by 15 to 20%, according to the World Economic Forum.
slides.footer: AI can optimise grids, model the climate, cut industrial waste and speed up clean energy. The same technology straining Ireland's grid could also help save it.

slides.text: The question isn't whether Ireland should have data centres. It's whether the right terms are being set.
slides.footer: Mandatory renewable energy, community benefit agreements, water rules and smarter locations could be the difference between a tech boom that helps the energy transition and one that derails it.
